title: Ἀλέξανδρος καὶ Μενέλαος
source: Homer, The Iliad, Greek text of D. B. Monro and T. W. Allen, Homeri Opera, tomi I–II, 3rd ed. (Oxford Classical Texts; Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1920), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg001.perseus-grc2, sha256 ae8b617018c6e5af. Text as printed: the edition sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: The Trojans advance with the clamour of cranes, the Achaeans in silence, and the dust rises under both armies. Alexander, who steps out before the Trojans in a leopard-skin and challenges the best of the Argives, sees Menelaus leap from his chariot, glad as a lion at a kill, and shrinks back into the ranks like a man who has seen a snake. Hector reviles him for a coward whose fair looks will not save him. Alexander accepts the reproach and proposes that both armies sit down while he and Menelaus fight alone for Helen and her goods, with oaths and a return home to follow. Hector is glad, halts the Trojans, holding his spear by the middle, and the Achaeans shoot at him until Agamemnon stops them, saying that Hector has something to say.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ κόσμηθεν ἅμ’ ἡγεμόνεσσιν ἕκαστοι,
Τρῶες μὲν κλαγγῇ τ’ ἐνοπῇ τ’ ἴσαν ὄρνιθες ὣς
ἠΰτε περ κλαγγὴ γεράνων πέλει οὐρανόθι πρό·
sentences.tr:
autar epei kosmēthen ham’ hēgemonessin hekastoi,
Trōes men klangēi t’ enopēi t’ isan ornithes hōs
ēÿte per klangē geranōn pelei ouranothi pro·
sentences.i: But when they were drawn up, each company with its leaders, the Trojans came on with clamour and shouting, like birds, just as the clamour of cranes sounds in the open sky;
sentences.n: αὐτὰρ ἐπεί is ‘but when’, and κόσμηθεν is the aorist passive of κοσμέω ‘arrange’, with the epic ending -θεν for -θησαν: ‘were drawn up’. ἕκαστοι ‘each’ is the subject of κόσμηθεν (the whole army, each company in turn; Τρῶες is the subject only of ἴσαν in the next line), and ἅμ’ ἡγεμόνεσσιν is ‘together with their leaders’. ἴσαν is the imperfect of εἶμι ‘go’, and ὄρνιθες ὣς ‘like birds’ has ὣς standing after the noun it goes with. The sentence turns into a simile at once: ἠΰτε περ is ‘just as’, and the cranes’ clamour is said to be οὐρανόθι πρό, where -θι marks place (‘in the sky’) and πρό is ‘forward, out in front’; the English ‘open sky’ renders the pair.

sentences.t:
αἵ τ’ ἐπεὶ οὖν χειμῶνα φύγον καὶ ἀθέσφατον ὄμβρον
κλαγγῇ ταί γε πέτονται ἐπ’ ὠκεανοῖο ῥοάων
ἀνδράσι Πυγμαίοισι φόνον καὶ κῆρα φέρουσαι·
sentences.tr:
hai t’ epei oun cheimōna phygon kai athesphaton ombron
klangēi tai ge petontai ep’ ōkeanoio rhoaōn
andrasi Pygmaioisi phonon kai kēra pherousai·
sentences.i: which, when they have fled the winter and the immense rain, fly with clamour toward the streams of Oceanus, bringing slaughter and death to Pygmy men;
sentences.n: αἵ is the relative ‘which’, picking up the cranes (γεράνων); the later ταί γε is a demonstrative ‘they’ that picks them up again. φύγον is an aorist without the augment (Attic ἔφυγον), and πέτονται is ‘they fly’. ὠκεανοῖο has the epic genitive -οιο (Attic -ου), and ἐπ’ with the genitive ῥοάων gives the direction, ‘toward the streams’ of Oceanus, the river thought of as flowing round the edge of the world. Πυγμαίοισι is the dative plural of Πυγμαῖοι, the Pygmies, a small people at war with the cranes. κῆρα is the accusative of κήρ ‘death-fate’, a different word from κῆρ ‘heart’; φέρουσαι is the feminine plural participle agreeing with ταί.

sentences.t: ἠέριαι δ’ ἄρα ταί γε κακὴν ἔριδα προφέρονται.
sentences.tr: ēeriai d’ ara tai ge kakēn erida propherontai.
sentences.l: and early, then, those same ones put forward evil strife.
sentences.i: and early in the day they bring on evil strife.
sentences.n: ἠέριαι ‘early’ is feminine plural to agree with the cranes. The word is old and disputed: it is usually taken as ‘in the early morning’, though a link with ἀήρ ‘mist’ is also proposed, and we keep the plain ‘early’. κακὴν ἔριδα is ‘evil strife’, and προφέρονται is the middle of προφέρω ‘put forward’: the cranes, having flown to the Pygmies, offer them a fight. The simile ends here, and the Achaeans are set against the noisy Trojans in the next unit.

sentences.t:
οἳ δ’ ἄρ’ ἴσαν σιγῇ μένεα πνείοντες Ἀχαιοὶ
ἐν θυμῷ μεμαῶτες ἀλεξέμεν ἀλλήλοισιν.
sentences.tr:
hoi d’ ar’ isan sigēi menea pneiontes Achaioi
en thymōi memaōtes alexemen allēloisin.
sentences.l:
But they, the Achaeans, went in silence, breathing might,
in spirit eager to defend one another.
sentences.i: But the Achaeans came on in silence, breathing might, eager in spirit to defend one another.
sentences.n: οἳ δ’ ἄρ’ ἴσαν ‘but they went’ sets the Achaeans against the Trojans of the first lines, and σιγῇ ‘in silence’ against their clamour. μένεα is the plural of μένος ‘might’, the surge of fighting strength, and πνείοντες is ‘breathing’. μεμαῶτες is the perfect participle of μέμαα ‘be eager’; the infinitive ἀλεξέμεν (epic for ἀλέξειν) ‘to defend’ takes the dative ἀλλήλοισιν ‘one another’.

sentences.t:
εὖτ’ ὄρεος κορυφῇσι Νότος κατέχευεν ὀμίχλην
ποιμέσιν οὔ τι φίλην, κλέπτῃ δέ τε νυκτὸς ἀμείνω,
τόσσόν τίς τ’ ἐπιλεύσσει ὅσον τ’ ἐπὶ λᾶαν ἵησιν·
sentences.tr:
eut’ oreos koryphēisi Notos katecheuen omichlēn
poimesin ou ti philēn, kleptēi de te nyktos ameinō,
tosson tis t’ epileussei hoson t’ epi laan hiēsin·
sentences.i: As when the South Wind pours mist down on a mountain’s peaks, no friend to shepherds but better than night for a thief, and a man sees just as far as he can throw a stone:
sentences.n: εὖτ’ ‘when, as when’ opens a second simile, about the dust the armies raise (it is finished at 13). The aorist κατέχευεν ‘has poured down’ is the timeless tense of a simile, and the English the English puts it in the present. ὄρεος is the epic genitive of ὄρος ‘mountain’, and κορυφῇσι the epic dative plural ‘on the peaks’. ποιμέσιν ‘for shepherds’ and κλέπτῃ ‘for a thief’ are datives of the person concerned; ἀμείνω is ἀμείνονα ‘better’, agreeing with ὀμίχλην ‘mist’. In the last line τόσσον … ὅσον is ‘so far … as far as’, and ἐπὶ … ἵησιν (from ἵημι) is ἐφίησιν ‘throws at’ split in two (tmesis), with λᾶαν ‘a stone’.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἄρα τῶν ὑπὸ ποσσὶ κονίσαλος ὄρνυτ’ ἀελλὴς
ἐρχομένων·
sentences.tr:
hōs ara tōn hypo possi konisalos ornyt’ aellēs
erchomenōn·
sentences.l:
so then beneath the feet of them a dust-cloud rose, stormy,
of them coming;
sentences.i: so under the feet of the marching men a stormy cloud of dust rose;
sentences.n: ὣς ἄρα ‘so then’ answers the εὖτ’ of the simile. κονίσαλος is ‘a cloud of dust’, ὄρνυτ’ is ὄρνυτο, the imperfect middle of ὄρνυμι, ‘rose’, and ἀελλής (from ἄελλα ‘storm-wind’) is ‘stormy’, in the same case as the dust-cloud. τῶν … ἐρχομένων is ‘of them as they came’, a genitive that says whose feet, with ὑπὸ ποσσί ‘under the feet’ (ποσσί is the epic dative plural of πούς).

sentences.t: μάλα δ’ ὦκα διέπρησσον πεδίοιο.
sentences.tr: mala d’ ōka dieprēsson pedioio.
sentences.l: and very quickly they were crossing the plain.
sentences.i: and they were crossing the plain very quickly.
sentences.n: The subject is still the marching armies. διέπρησσον is the imperfect of διαπρήσσω ‘make one’s way through’, and it takes the genitive πεδίοιο (epic for πεδίου) ‘the plain’, the genitive of the ground covered. μάλα … ὦκα is ‘very quickly’.

sentences.t:
οἳ δ’ ὅτε δὴ σχεδὸν ἦσαν ἐπ’ ἀλλήλοισιν ἰόντες,
Τρωσὶν μὲν προμάχιζεν Ἀλέξανδρος θεοειδὴς
παρδαλέην ὤμοισιν ἔχων καὶ καμπύλα τόξα
καὶ ξίφος·
sentences.tr:
hoi d’ hote dē schedon ēsan ep’ allēloisin iontes,
Trōsin men promachizen Alexandros theoeidēs
pardaleēn ōmoisin echōn kai kampyla toxa
kai xiphos·
sentences.i: And when they were near, advancing on one another, Alexander, godlike in form, was fighting in the front rank for the Trojans, with a leopard’s skin on his shoulders, and a curved bow and a sword;
sentences.n: Alexander is the Trojan prince the poem also calls Paris; here the poet uses only the name Alexander, and Hector will address him as Δύσπαρι at 39. οἳ δ’ ὅτε δὴ … ἦσαν ‘and when they were’ has σχεδόν ‘near’ and ἰόντες (from εἶμι) ‘going, advancing’. προμάχιζεν is the imperfect of προμαχίζω ‘fight in the front rank’, and Τρωσίν is dative ‘for the Trojans’. θεοειδής ‘godlike in form’ is the stock epithet (θεός + εἶδος). παρδαλέην is feminine, ‘of a leopard’, and stands as a noun for the skin; ἔχων ‘having’ governs it, the bow and the sword. τόξα is plural in form, but one bow is meant; the sentence goes on after the stop.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ δοῦρε δύω κεκορυθμένα χαλκῷ
πάλλων Ἀργείων προκαλίζετο πάντας ἀρίστους
ἀντίβιον μαχέσασθαι ἐν αἰνῇ δηϊοτῆτι.
sentences.tr:
autar doure dyō kekorythmena chalkōi
pallōn Argeiōn prokalizeto pantas aristous
antibion machesasthai en ainēi dēïotēti.
sentences.l:
and two spears armed with bronze
brandishing, he challenged of the Argives all the best
in open opposition to fight in fearsome fighting.
sentences.i: and brandishing two spears armed with bronze, he challenged all the best of the Argives to fight him in open opposition, in fearsome fighting.
sentences.n: αὐτάρ here simply adds the next thing: the spears. δοῦρε is the dual of δόρυ ‘spear’, with δύω ‘two’. κεκορυθμένα is a perfect passive participle (from κόρυς ‘helmet’, so literally ‘helmeted’) and is read as ‘armed with bronze’. πάλλων is ‘brandishing’, and προκαλίζετο ‘called out, challenged’ takes πάντας ἀρίστους ‘all the best men’ with the partitive genitive Ἀργείων. ἀντίβιον ‘in open opposition’ is an adverb, and μαχέσασθαι an aorist infinitive ‘to fight’. αἰνῇ δηϊοτῆτι is the dative of δηϊοτής ‘fighting’, ‘in fearsome fighting’.

sentences.t:
τὸν δ’ ὡς οὖν ἐνόησεν ἀρηΐφιλος Μενέλαος
ἐρχόμενον προπάροιθεν ὁμίλου μακρὰ βιβάντα,
ὥς τε λέων ἐχάρη μεγάλῳ ἐπὶ σώματι κύρσας
εὑρὼν ἢ ἔλαφον κεραὸν ἢ ἄγριον αἶγα
πεινάων·
sentences.tr:
ton d’ hōs oun enoēsen arēïphilos Menelaos
erchomenon proparoithen homilou makra bibanta,
hōs te leōn echarē megalōi epi sōmati kyrsas
heurōn ē elaphon keraon ē agrion aiga
peinaōn·
sentences.l:
Him then as he noticed, Ares-loved Menelaus,
coming in front of the throng with long strides,
like a lion he rejoiced, upon a great body having chanced,
having found either a horned deer or a wild goat,
hungry;
sentences.i: And when Menelaus, dear to Ares, noticed him coming out in front of the throng with long strides, he rejoiced like a lion that has come upon a great carcass, finding a horned deer or a wild goat when he is hungry;
sentences.n: τὸν δ’ ὡς οὖν ἐνόησεν ‘and when he noticed him’ is the first of two matching lines (compare 30), with the participles ἐρχόμενον and βιβάντα (from βίβημι ‘stride’) agreeing with τόν: ‘coming … taking long strides’. προπάροιθεν ὁμίλου is ‘in front of the throng’, and μακρά is a neuter plural used as an adverb. ὥς τε λέων ἐχάρη is a simile with the aorist ἐχάρη ‘rejoiced’ (a timeless tense; the English keeps ‘rejoiced’ in the narrative and puts the lion’s acts in the present). κύρσας is the aorist participle of κύρω ‘come upon’ with the dative, and σῶμα in Homer is a dead body, here the carcass of the beast; εὑρών is ‘finding’, κεραόν ‘horned’, and πεινάων (an uncontracted πεινῶν) ‘being hungry’ belongs to the lion.

sentences.t:
μάλα γάρ τε κατεσθίει, εἴ περ ἂν αὐτὸν
σεύωνται ταχέες τε κύνες θαλεροί τ’ αἰζηοί·
sentences.tr:
mala gar te katesthiei, ei per an auton
seuōntai tachees te kynes thaleroi t’ aizēoi·
sentences.l:
for he devours greatly, even if him
they set upon, swift dogs and blooming vigorous men;
sentences.i: for he devours it greedily, even if swift dogs and blooming, vigorous men rush at him;
sentences.n: The subject is the lion. μάλα … κατεσθίει is ‘devours greatly’; εἴ περ ἄν with the subjunctive σεύωνται is ‘even if they should rush’ (ἄν here does the work of Attic ἐάν). σεύομαι is the middle ‘rush, dart’, and with αὐτόν ‘him’ it means ‘rush at’. ταχέες is the uncontracted ταχεῖς ‘swift’, and αἰζηοί are ‘vigorous young men’, with θαλεροί ‘blooming’, the same word as at 53.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἐχάρη Μενέλαος Ἀλέξανδρον θεοειδέα
ὀφθαλμοῖσιν ἰδών·
sentences.tr:
hōs echarē Menelaos Alexandron theoeidea
ophthalmoisin idōn·
sentences.l:
so rejoiced Menelaus, Alexander godlike-in-form
with eyes having seen;
sentences.i: So Menelaus rejoiced when he saw Alexander, godlike in form, with his eyes;
sentences.n: ὣς ἐχάρη ‘so he rejoiced’ closes the simile; ἐχάρη is the aorist of χαίρω. ἰδών is the aorist participle of εἶδον ‘see’, and ὀφθαλμοῖσιν is ‘with eyes’, a dative of means. Ἀλέξανδρον θεοειδέα is the accusative, with the stock epithet.

sentences.t: φάτο γὰρ τίσεσθαι ἀλείτην·
sentences.tr: phato gar tisesthai aleitēn·
sentences.l: for he thought to take vengeance on the offender;
sentences.i: for he thought he would take vengeance on the offender;
sentences.n: φάτο is the past middle of φημί (= ἔφατο), here ‘he said (to himself)’, that is ‘thought’, followed by the future infinitive τίσεσθαι (from τίνυμαι) ‘to take vengeance on’. ἀλείτην is the accusative of ἀλείτης ‘offender’, the one who has wronged him; the wrong is Helen’s abduction, which Menelaus’ thought leaves unsaid.

sentences.t: αὐτίκα δ’ ἐξ ὀχέων σὺν τεύχεσιν ἆλτο χαμᾶζε.
sentences.tr: autika d’ ex ocheōn syn teuchesin alto chamaze.
sentences.l: and at once from the chariot, with his armour, he leapt to the ground.
sentences.i: and at once he leapt from his chariot to the ground in his armour.
sentences.n: ἐξ ὀχέων is ‘from the chariot’; ὄχεα is a neuter plural used for one chariot. σὺν τεύχεσιν ‘with his armour’ shows he jumped down fully armed. ἆλτο is the aorist of ἅλλομαι ‘leap’, and χαμᾶζε ‘to the ground’ has the ending -ζε of direction (like -δε).

sentences.t:
τὸν δ’ ὡς οὖν ἐνόησεν Ἀλέξανδρος θεοειδὴς
ἐν προμάχοισι φανέντα, κατεπλήγη φίλον ἦτορ,
ἂψ δ’ ἑτάρων εἰς ἔθνος ἐχάζετο κῆρ’ ἀλεείνων.
sentences.tr:
ton d’ hōs oun enoēsen Alexandros theoeidēs
en promachoisi phanenta, kateplēgē philon ētor,
aps d’ hetarōn eis ethnos echazeto kēr’ aleeinōn.
sentences.l:
Him then as he noticed, Alexander godlike-in-form,
appearing among the front-fighters, he was struck in his dear heart,
and back to the company of his companions he drew away, death-fate avoiding.
sentences.i: And when Alexander, godlike in form, noticed him appear among the foremost fighters, he was stricken at the heart, and drew back into the company of his companions, shunning death.
sentences.n: τὸν δ’ ὡς οὖν ἐνόησεν repeats the line-opening of 21, now with Alexander as subject. φανέντα is the aorist passive participle of φαίνω, ‘having appeared’. προμάχοισι ‘front-fighters’ are the men who fight before the line. κατεπλήγη is the aorist passive of καταπλήσσω ‘strike, stun’, and φίλον ἦτορ ‘in his dear heart’ is an accusative of respect. ἔθνος is ‘company’, ἑτάρων the epic form of ἑταίρων ‘companions’, and ἐχάζετο the imperfect of χάζομαι ‘draw back’. κῆρ’ is κῆρα, the accusative of κήρ ‘death-fate’ with the final vowel elided; ἀλεείνων is ‘avoiding’.

sentences.t:
ὡς δ’ ὅτε τίς τε δράκοντα ἰδὼν παλίνορσος ἀπέστη
οὔρεος ἐν βήσσῃς, ὑπό τε τρόμος ἔλλαβε γυῖα,
ἂψ δ’ ἀνεχώρησεν, ὦχρός τέ μιν εἷλε παρειάς,
sentences.tr:
hōs d’ hote tis te drakonta idōn palinorsos apestē
oureos en bēssēis, hypo te tromos ellabe guia,
aps d’ anechōrēsen, ōchros te min heile pareias,
sentences.l:
And as when someone, a snake having seen, starting-back stood away
in the glens of a mountain, and beneath him trembling took his limbs,
and back he withdrew, and pallor took him by the cheeks,
sentences.i: And as when a man sees a snake and starts back in the glens of a mountain, and trembling takes hold of his limbs from beneath, and he withdraws, and pallor seizes his cheeks,
sentences.n: A simile for Alexander’s retreat. ὡς δ’ ὅτε τίς τε is ‘and as when someone’, and the aorists (ἀπέστη, ἔλλαβε, ἀνεχώρησεν, εἷλε) are timeless, so the English puts them in the present. παλίνορσος is ‘starting back’ (πάλιν ‘back’ + ὄρνυμι). οὔρεος is the epic genitive of ὄρος, and βήσσῃς the epic dative plural of βῆσσα ‘glen’. ὑπό is an adverb, ‘from beneath’, with τρόμος ‘trembling’ and γυῖα ‘limbs’ (ἔλλαβε has a doubled λ for the metre). ὦχρος is ‘pallor’; μιν is the man, and παρειάς ‘cheeks’ the part affected, a double accusative of whole and part.

sentences.t:
ὣς αὖτις καθ’ ὅμιλον ἔδυ Τρώων ἀγερώχων
δείσας Ἀτρέος υἱὸν Ἀλέξανδρος θεοειδής.
sentences.tr:
hōs autis kath’ homilon edy Trōōn agerōchōn
deisas Atreos huion Alexandros theoeidēs.
sentences.l:
so back again into the throng went down of the lofty Trojans
having feared the son of Atreus, Alexander godlike-in-form.
sentences.i: so Alexander, godlike in form, sank back into the throng of the lofty Trojans, in fear of Atreus’ son.
sentences.n: ὣς αὖτις ‘so again, back’ answers the simile. ἔδυ is the aorist of δύω ‘go down into, sink’, and καθ’ ὅμιλον ‘down into the throng’ with the genitive Τρώων. ἀγερώχων ‘lofty’ is the stock epithet of the Trojans here, a word whose meaning is not known. δείσας is the aorist participle of δείδω ‘fear’, with Ἀτρέος υἱόν ‘the son of Atreus’, Menelaus; Ἀτρέος is the epic genitive of Ἀτρεύς.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ Ἕκτωρ νείκεσσεν ἰδὼν αἰσχροῖς ἐπέεσσιν·
sentences.tr: ton d’ Hektōr neikessen idōn aischrois epeessin·
sentences.l: Him then Hector reviled, seeing him, with shameful words:
sentences.i: And Hector, seeing him, reviled him with shameful words:
sentences.n: νείκεσσεν is the aorist of νεικέω ‘revile’, and ἰδών ‘having seen’ gives the occasion. αἰσχροῖς ἐπέεσσιν is ‘with shameful words’, ἐπέεσσιν being the epic dative plural of ἔπος. Hector’s speech follows, with the Greek unmarked.

sentences.t:
Δύσπαρι εἶδος ἄριστε γυναιμανὲς ἠπεροπευτὰ
αἴθ’ ὄφελες ἄγονός τ’ ἔμεναι ἄγαμός τ’ ἀπολέσθαι·
sentences.tr:
Dyspari eidos ariste gynaimanes ēperopeuta
aith’ opheles agonos t’ emenai agamos t’ apolesthai·
sentences.l:
“Ill-Paris, best in form, woman-mad, deceiver,
would that you had been unborn, and had perished unwed;
sentences.i: “Wretched Paris, fairest in looks, mad for women, deceiver, if only you had never been born, and had died unwed;
sentences.n: Hector uses the other name Δύσπαρι, the vocative of Δύσπαρις, in which δυσ- ‘ill, bad’ is put before Πάρις as an insult; it is the same man as Alexander. The string of vocatives is εἶδος ἄριστε ‘best in form’ (εἶδος an accusative of respect), γυναιμανές ‘mad for women’ (γυνή + μαίνομαι), and ἠπεροπευτά ‘deceiver’. αἴθ’ is αἴθε ‘if only’, and ὄφελες (from ὀφέλλω ‘owe, ought’) with an infinitive is a wish that cannot now be met: ‘you ought to have been’. ἄγονος is ‘unborn’, though ‘childless’ is also possible, and ἄγαμος ‘unmarried’; ἔμεναι is ‘to be’ and ἀπολέσθαι the aorist middle ‘to perish’.

sentences.t:
καί κε τὸ βουλοίμην, καί κεν πολὺ κέρδιον ἦεν
ἢ οὕτω λώβην τ’ ἔμεναι καὶ ὑπόψιον ἄλλων.
sentences.tr:
kai ke to bouloimēn, kai ken poly kerdion ēen
ē houtō lōbēn t’ emenai kai hypopsion allōn.
sentences.l:
and that I would wish, and much better it would be
than thus an outrage to be and one looked at askance by others.
sentences.i: I would wish that, and it would be far better than that you should be as you are, an outrage and a man looked at askance by others.
sentences.n: τὸ βουλοίμην ‘I should wish that’ has the optative βουλοίμην, and καί κεν … ἦεν (ἦεν = ἦν) is ‘and it would be’. κέρδιον ‘better’ is a comparative from κέρδος ‘gain’, used simply as ‘better’. ἢ οὕτω … ἔμεναι is ‘than to be thus’, with the unspoken subject ‘you’; λώβην ‘outrage’ is the accusative of λώβη. ὑπόψιον is ὑπό + ὄψ ‘sight’, ‘looked at from under’, that is askance or with suspicion, and ἄλλων is a genitive ‘by others’.

sentences.t:
ἦ που καγχαλόωσι κάρη κομόωντες Ἀχαιοὶ
φάντες ἀριστῆα πρόμον ἔμμεναι, οὕνεκα καλὸν
εἶδος ἔπ’, ἀλλ’ οὐκ ἔστι βίη φρεσὶν οὐδέ τις ἀλκή.
sentences.tr:
ē pou kanchaloōsi karē komoōntes Achaioi
phantes aristēa promon emmenai, houneka kalon
eidos ep’, all’ ouk esti biē phresin oude tis alkē.
sentences.l:
Truly, I suppose, the long-haired-of-head Achaeans are exulting,
saying that a best man, a foremost fighter, is there, because a fair
form is upon him, but there is no force in his mind nor any might.
sentences.i: Surely the long-haired Achaeans are exulting, saying that he is a best man, a foremost fighter, because a fair form is upon him, but there is no force in his mind, nor any might.
sentences.n: ἦ που is ‘truly, I suppose, surely’, and καγχαλόωσι is the uncontracted καγχαλῶσι ‘they exult’. κάρη κομόωντες is the stock epithet ‘long-haired’ (literally ‘wearing the hair long on the head’). φάντες is the present participle of φημί, ‘saying’, and ἔμμεναι is ‘to be’, with ‘he’ (Alexander) understood. ἀριστῆα πρόμον is ‘a best man, a foremost fighter’; πρόμος is the man who fights in front. οὕνεκα is ‘because’, ἔπ’ is ἔπι = ἔπεστι ‘is upon him’, and βίη φρεσίν is ‘force in the mind’. The last clause, from ἀλλ’, is Hector’s own judgement and not the Achaeans’ words.

sentences.t:
ἦ τοιόσδε ἐὼν ἐν ποντοπόροισι νέεσσι
πόντον ἐπιπλώσας, ἑτάρους ἐρίηρας ἀγείρας,
μιχθεὶς ἀλλοδαποῖσι γυναῖκ’ εὐειδέ’ ἀνῆγες
ἐξ ἀπίης γαίης νυὸν ἀνδρῶν αἰχμητάων
πατρί τε σῷ μέγα πῆμα πόληΐ τε παντί τε δήμῳ,
sentences.tr:
ē toiosde eōn en pontoporoisi neessi
ponton epiplōsas, hetarous eriēras ageiras,
michtheis allodapoisi gynaik’ eueide’ anēges
ex apiēs gaiēs nyon andrōn aichmētaōn
patri te sōi mega pēma polēï te panti te dēmōi,
sentences.l:
Was it as such a man, on sea-crossing ships
having sailed over the sea, trusty companions having gathered,
having mingled with foreigners, that a fair-formed woman you led away
from a distant land, a bride of men, spearmen,
to your father a great woe, and to the city and to all the land,
sentences.i: Was it, being such a man as you are, that you sailed over the sea in sea-crossing ships, gathered trusty companions, and, mingling with foreigners, led away a fair-formed woman from a distant land, a bride of spearmen, a great woe to your father, to the city and to all the land,
sentences.n: ἦ opens a question, and the question mark comes only at 51; the sentence is one long question, ἦ τοιόσδε ἐὼν … ἀνῆγες, ‘being such a man, did you lead away …?’. The three participles ἐπιπλώσας (from ἐπιπλέω ‘sail over’), ἀγείρας ‘having gathered’ and μιχθείς ‘having mingled’ (aorist passive of μίγνυμι, with the dative ἀλλοδαποῖσι ‘strangers’) lead up to the verb ἀνῆγες, ‘you led away’ (literally ‘led up’, also the verb for putting to sea). εὐειδέ’ is εὐειδέα ‘fair-formed’, ἀπίης ‘distant’ (the ancient explanation; the sense is not certain), and νυόν ‘bride’; ἀνδρῶν αἰχμητάων is ‘of men, spearmen’, with the epic genitive plural -άων. The datives πατρί, πόληΐ and δήμῳ all depend on πῆμα ‘woe’, and δῆμος is the land with its people.

sentences.t: δυσμενέσιν μὲν χάρμα, κατηφείην δὲ σοὶ αὐτῷ;
sentences.tr: dysmenesin men charma, katēpheiēn de soi autōi;
sentences.l: to the ill-disposed a joy, but dejection to you yourself?
sentences.i: a joy to the ill-disposed, but dejection to yourself?
sentences.n: This ends the long question begun at 46, with the nouns in apposition to πῆμα: δυσμενέσιν ‘to the ill-disposed’ (the dative plural of δυσμενής) is set against σοὶ αὐτῷ ‘to you yourself’, and χάρμα ‘joy’ against κατηφείην ‘dejection’, the downcast look of shame.

sentences.t: οὐκ ἂν δὴ μείνειας ἀρηΐφιλον Μενέλαον;
sentences.tr: ouk an dē meineias arēïphilon Menelaon;
sentences.l: Would you not, then, await Ares-loved Menelaus?
sentences.i: Would you not stand your ground against Menelaus, dear to Ares?
sentences.n: οὐκ ἂν δὴ μείνειας is a question with the optative, ‘would you not, then, …?’. μείνειας is the aorist of μένω, which with an accusative means ‘await’ and so ‘stand against’. ἀρηΐφιλος is the stock epithet, ‘dear to Ares’.

sentences.t: γνοίης χ’ οἵου φωτὸς ἔχεις θαλερὴν παράκοιτιν·
sentences.tr: gnoiēs ch’ hoiou phōtos echeis thalerēn parakoitin·
sentences.l: you would know of what man you hold the blooming consort;
sentences.i: You would learn what sort of man it is whose blooming wife you keep;
sentences.n: γνοίης is the aorist optative of γιγνώσκω, and χ’ is κε, its κ aspirated before the rough breathing of οἵου; together they give ‘you would come to know’. οἵου φωτός is ‘of what sort of man’, a genitive that depends on παράκοιτιν (‘the wife of what sort of man’), the whole being the object of γνοίης; θαλερήν is ‘blooming’, and παράκοιτις (literally ‘one who lies beside’) is a word for a wife, ‘consort’ in the literal line.

sentences.t:
οὐκ ἄν τοι χραίσμῃ κίθαρις τά τε δῶρ’ Ἀφροδίτης
ἥ τε κόμη τό τε εἶδος ὅτ’ ἐν κονίῃσι μιγείης.
sentences.tr:
ouk an toi chraismēi kitharis ta te dōr’ Aphroditēs
hē te komē to te eidos hot’ en koniēisi migeiēs.
sentences.l:
not would avail you the lyre and the gifts of Aphrodite,
both the hair and the form, when in the dust you were mingled.
sentences.i: The lyre would be no help to you, nor the gifts of Aphrodite, your hair and your looks, when you were mingled with the dust.
sentences.n: οὐκ ἄν τοι χραίσμῃ is ‘would not avail you’: χραίσμῃ is the aorist subjunctive of χραισμέω with ἄν, and τοι is σοι. The gifts are named by apposition: ἥ τε κόμη τό τε εἶδος is ‘both the hair and the form’, with τε … τε as ‘both … and’ and ἥ, τό the article-forms (pronouns in origin) before each noun. μιγείης is the aorist passive optative of μίγνυμι, ‘you were mingled’, here with κονίῃσι ‘dust’ in the plural: the picture is of a man rolled in the dust of the fight. κίθαρις is the lyre.

sentences.t: ἀλλὰ μάλα Τρῶες δειδήμονες·
sentences.tr: alla mala Trōes deidēmones·
sentences.l: but very timid are the Trojans;
sentences.i: But the Trojans are very timid;
sentences.n: ἀλλὰ μάλα … is ‘but very’, and δειδήμονες ‘timid’ is related to δείδω ‘fear’; the formation of the word is not fully clear. Hector means that the Trojans will not punish Alexander, and the next lines say what he deserves.

sentences.t:
ἦ τέ κεν ἤδη
λάϊνον ἕσσο χιτῶνα κακῶν ἕνεχ’ ὅσσα ἔοργας.
sentences.tr:
ē te ken ēdē
laïnon hesso chitōna kakōn henech’ hossa eorgas.
sentences.l:
surely indeed already
a stone tunic you would have put on, for the sake of the evils, all you have done.”
sentences.i: by now you would have put on a tunic of stone for all the evil you have done.”
sentences.n: ἦ τέ κεν ἤδη is ‘surely, by now’, with κεν and the aorist ἕσσο (the middle of ἕννυμι ‘put on’, 2nd singular), ‘you would have put on’. λάϊνον χιτῶνα, a ‘tunic of stone’, is a figure for being stoned to death. κακῶν ἕνεχ’ ὅσσα ἔοργας is ‘because of the evils, all that you have done’: ἕνεχ’ is ἕνεκα ‘on account of’ and ἔοργας the perfect of ἔρδω ‘do’. The timid Trojans, he says, are all that has so far saved Alexander from this.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπεν Ἀλέξανδρος θεοειδής·
sentences.tr: ton d’ aute proseeipen Alexandros theoeidēs·
sentences.l: Him then in turn addressed Alexander godlike-in-form:
sentences.i: Then Alexander, godlike in form, spoke to him in turn:
sentences.n: τὸν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπεν is the formula for a reply, ‘and him in turn he addressed’ (προσέειπεν ‘spoke to’, with movable -ν before the vowel). The stock epithet θεοειδής follows the name.

sentences.t: Ἕκτορ ἐπεί με κατ’ αἶσαν ἐνείκεσας οὐδ’ ὑπὲρ αἶσαν·
sentences.tr: Hektor epei me kat’ aisan eneikesas oud’ hyper aisan·
sentences.l: “Hector, since me in due measure you reviled and not beyond due measure;
sentences.i: “Hector, since you have reviled me in due measure, and not beyond it;
sentences.n: Hector is addressed with the vocative Ἕκτορ. ἐπεί με … ἐνείκεσας is ‘since you reviled me’, an aorist (ἐνείκεσας = ἐ- + νείκεσας, from νεικέω) with κατ’ αἶσαν ‘in due measure’, literally ‘according to due portion’, set against ὑπὲρ αἶσαν ‘beyond it’. The ἐπεί clause gives the ground but has no main clause: Alexander breaks off and goes straight on, in the next line, to the axe.

sentences.t:
αἰεί τοι κραδίη πέλεκυς ὥς ἐστιν ἀτειρὴς
ὅς τ’ εἶσιν διὰ δουρὸς ὑπ’ ἀνέρος ὅς ῥά τε τέχνῃ
νήϊον ἐκτάμνῃσιν, ὀφέλλει δ’ ἀνδρὸς ἐρωήν·
sentences.tr:
aiei toi kradiē pelekys hōs estin ateirēs
hos t’ eisin dia douros hyp’ aneros hos rha te technēi
nēïon ektamnēisin, ophellei d’ andros erōēn·
sentences.i: Your heart is always unwearied, like an axe that goes through timber when a man works it, a man who skilfully hews out ship-timber, and it adds to the man’s force;
sentences.n: αἰεί ‘always’ and τοι ‘to you’ (a dative that comes to mean ‘your’) frame the comparison: κραδίη ‘heart’ is the subject, πέλεκυς ὥς ‘like an axe’ the picture, and ἀτειρής ‘unwearied’ the shared word. The axe is ὅς τ’ εἶσιν διὰ δουρός ‘which goes through timber’ (δόρυ here is wood, not a spear), ὑπ’ ἀνέρος ‘under a man’, that is worked by him, ὅς … τέχνῃ ‘who by skill’ ἐκτάμνῃσιν (subjunctive of ἐκτάμνω ‘cut out’) νήϊον ‘ship-timber’. ὀφέλλει is ‘increases’, ἀνδρὸς ἐρωήν ‘the man’s rush’, his force: the sharper the axe, the more the man’s effort tells.

sentences.t: ὣς σοὶ ἐνὶ στήθεσσιν ἀτάρβητος νόος ἐστί·
sentences.tr: hōs soi eni stēthessin atarbētos noos esti·
sentences.l: so in you, in your breast, fearless is the mind;
sentences.i: so there is a fearless mind in your breast;
sentences.n: ὣς answers the ὥς of the axe. σοὶ ἐνὶ στήθεσσιν is ‘in your breast’, with the epic dative plural στήθεσσιν, and νόος is the uncontracted form of νοῦς ‘mind’. ἀτάρβητος ‘fearless’ is ‘not to be frightened’ (ἀ- + ταρβέω), and is said in praise: Alexander grants Hector his courage.

sentences.t: μή μοι δῶρ’ ἐρατὰ πρόφερε χρυσέης Ἀφροδίτης·
sentences.tr: mē moi dōr’ erata prophere chryseēs Aphroditēs·
sentences.l: do not bring forward to me the lovely gifts of golden Aphrodite;
sentences.i: do not bring up against me the lovely gifts of golden Aphrodite;
sentences.n: μή with the imperative πρόφερε (from προφέρω ‘bring forward’) is ‘do not bring forward’, here ‘hold up against me’. ἐρατά ‘lovely’ describes the gifts, and χρυσέης is the genitive of χρυσέη ‘golden’, uncontracted (Attic χρυσῆς). The gifts are the beauty and the lyre that Hector mocked at 54–55.

sentences.t:
οὔ τοι ἀπόβλητ’ ἐστὶ θεῶν ἐρικυδέα δῶρα
ὅσσά κεν αὐτοὶ δῶσιν, ἑκὼν δ’ οὐκ ἄν τις ἕλοιτο·
sentences.tr:
ou toi apoblēt’ esti theōn erikydea dōra
hossa ken autoi dōsin, hekōn d’ ouk an tis heloito·
sentences.l:
not to be thrown away are the glorious gifts of the gods,
whatever they themselves may give, but willingly no one would choose them;
sentences.i: The glorious gifts of the gods are not to be thrown away, whatever they themselves may give, but of his own will no one would choose them;
sentences.n: ἀπόβλητα is a verbal adjective, ‘to be thrown away’, with οὔ τοι ‘surely not’. ἐρικυδέα ‘glorious’ is the neuter plural, and ὅσσα κεν … δῶσιν is ‘whatever they may give’ (aorist subjunctive of δίδωμι). ἑκών ‘willingly’ goes with οὐκ ἄν τις ἕλοιτο ‘no one would choose’; the sense is that a man cannot take such gifts by wishing, only by the gods’ giving.

sentences.t:
νῦν αὖτ’ εἴ μ’ ἐθέλεις πολεμίζειν ἠδὲ μάχεσθαι,
ἄλλους μὲν κάθισον Τρῶας καὶ πάντας Ἀχαιούς,
αὐτὰρ ἔμ’ ἐν μέσσῳ καὶ ἀρηΐφιλον Μενέλαον
συμβάλετ’ ἀμφ’ Ἑλένῃ καὶ κτήμασι πᾶσι μάχεσθαι·
sentences.tr:
nyn aut’ ei m’ etheleis polemizein ēde machesthai,
allous men kathison Trōas kai pantas Achaious,
autar em’ en messōi kai arēïphilon Menelaon
symbalet’ amph’ Helenēi kai ktēmasi pasi machesthai·
sentences.l:
Now again, if you want me to wage war and to fight,
the others make sit, the Trojans and all the Achaeans,
but me in the middle and Ares-loved Menelaus
set together to fight over Helen and all the possessions;
sentences.i: Now then, if you want me to wage war and to fight, make all the others sit down, the Trojans and all the Achaeans, and set me in the middle with Menelaus, dear to Ares, to fight together over Helen and all the possessions;
sentences.n: νῦν αὖτ’ (αὖτε) is ‘now again’, and εἴ μ’ ἐθέλεις … is ‘if you want me to’ with the two infinitives πολεμίζειν ἠδὲ μάχεσθαι ‘to wage war and to fight’. κάθισον is the singular imperative of καθίζω used with an object, ‘make sit’: Hector is asked to do it; then συμβάλετ’ is plural, ‘set together’, without saying who is addressed. ἄλλους μὲν … αὐτὰρ ἔμ’ ‘the others … but me’ is a contrast, and ἀμφ’ Ἑλένῃ means ‘about, over Helen’. κτήμασι πᾶσι are all the possessions carried off with her. ἀρηΐφιλον is the stock epithet.

sentences.t:
ὁππότερος δέ κε νικήσῃ κρείσσων τε γένηται,
κτήμαθ’ ἑλὼν εὖ πάντα γυναῖκά τε οἴκαδ’ ἀγέσθω·
sentences.tr:
hoppoteros de ke nikēsēi kreissōn te genētai,
ktēmath’ helōn eu panta gynaika te oikad’ agesthō·
sentences.l:
and whichever of the two wins and proves the stronger,
the possessions having taken, well, all, and the woman, home let him lead;
sentences.i: and whichever of the two wins and proves the stronger, let him properly take all the possessions and lead the woman home;
sentences.n: The first line is the same as a line of the Odyssey, where it stands in a different sentence. ὁππότερος is ‘whichever of two’, with νικήσῃ and γένηται in the subjunctive after κε. κτήμαθ’ is κτήματα ‘possessions’, and ἑλών the aorist participle of αἱρέω ‘having taken’. εὖ ‘well, properly’ is joined to ἑλών, and ἀγέσθω is the middle imperative of ἄγω, ‘let him lead (for himself), take home’; οἴκαδε is ‘homeward’, with the -δε of direction.

sentences.t:
οἳ δ’ ἄλλοι φιλότητα καὶ ὅρκια πιστὰ ταμόντες
ναίοιτε Τροίην ἐριβώλακα, τοὶ δὲ νεέσθων
Ἄργος ἐς ἱππόβοτον καὶ Ἀχαιΐδα καλλιγύναικα.
sentences.tr:
hoi d’ alloi philotēta kai horkia pista tamontes
naioite Troiēn eribōlaka, toi de neesthōn
Argos es hippoboton kai Achaiïda kalligynaika.
sentences.l:
and you others, friendship and faithful oaths having cut,
may you dwell in rich-soiled Troy, and let them go back
to Argos horse-pasturing and Achaea of the fair women.”
sentences.i: and the rest of you, having made friendship and sworn faithful oaths, may you live in rich-soiled Troy, and let them go back to horse-pasturing Argos and to Achaea of the fair women.”
sentences.n: οἳ δ’ ἄλλοι is ‘and you others’, the Trojans (and their allies) left over; the verb to which it belongs is ναίοιτε, the second-person plural optative of ναίω ‘dwell’, a wish used as a command. φιλότητα καὶ ὅρκια πιστὰ ταμόντες is ‘having cut friendship and faithful oaths’, ταμόντες the aorist participle of τέμνω; ‘cutting’ oaths comes from cutting the victims. τοὶ δέ is ‘and they’ (the Achaeans), with the imperative νεέσθων ‘let them go back’. ἐριβώλακα ‘rich-soiled’, ἱππόβοτον ‘horse-pasturing’ and καλλιγύναικα ‘of the fair women’ are stock epithets; Ἄργος names the Achaeans’ homeland, and Ἀχαιΐδα is ‘Achaea’, the land of the Achaeans.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφαθ’, Ἕκτωρ δ’ αὖτ’ ἐχάρη μέγα μῦθον ἀκούσας,
sentences.tr: hōs ephath’, Hektōr d’ aut’ echarē mega mython akousas,
sentences.l: So he spoke, and Hector in turn rejoiced greatly, the speech having heard,
sentences.i: So he spoke, and Hector rejoiced greatly to hear the speech,
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφαθ’ is the stock closing, ‘so he spoke’; ἔφαθ’ is ἔφατο with its τ made θ before the rough breathing of Ἕκτωρ. δ’ αὖτ’ ‘and in his turn’ answers the speech, ἐχάρη (aorist of χαίρω) is ‘rejoiced’, and ἀκούσας the aorist participle ‘having heard’ with the object μῦθον ‘speech’. μέγα is an adverb, ‘greatly’.

sentences.t:
καί ῥ’ ἐς μέσσον ἰὼν Τρώων ἀνέεργε φάλαγγας
μέσσου δουρὸς ἑλών·
sentences.tr:
kai rh’ es messon iōn Trōōn aneerge phalangas
messou douros helōn·
sentences.l:
and going into the middle he held back the battle-lines of the Trojans,
by the middle of his spear having taken hold;
sentences.i: and going into the middle he held back the Trojan battle-lines, grasping his spear by the middle;
sentences.n: καί ῥ’ is καὶ ἄρα ‘and then’. ἐς μέσσον ἰών is ‘going into the middle’ between the armies, and ἀνέεργε the imperfect of ἀνέργω ‘hold back’ (Attic ἀνεῖργε); φάλαγγας are the ‘battle-lines’. μέσσου δουρὸς ἑλών is ‘having taken hold of the spear by the middle’, with the genitive of the part grasped.

sentences.t: τοὶ δ’ ἱδρύνθησαν ἅπαντες.
sentences.tr: toi d’ hidrynthēsan hapantes.
sentences.l: and they were seated, all.
sentences.i: and they all sat down.
sentences.n: τοί is the article used as ‘they’ (the Trojans), and ἱδρύνθησαν is the aorist passive of ἱδρύω ‘make sit, settle’, so ‘were seated’; ἅπαντες ‘all’ is the emphatic form of πάντες.

sentences.t:
τῷ δ’ ἐπετοξάζοντο κάρη κομόωντες Ἀχαιοὶ
ἰοῖσίν τε τιτυσκόμενοι λάεσσί τ’ ἔβαλλον·
sentences.tr:
tōi d’ epetoxazonto karē komoōntes Achaioi
ioisin te tityskomenoi laessi t’ eballon·
sentences.l:
At him were aiming-with-bows the long-haired-of-head Achaeans,
with arrows taking aim, and with stones they kept pelting;
sentences.i: But the long-haired Achaeans kept shooting at him, aiming with arrows and pelting him with stones;
sentences.n: τῷ is ‘at him’, Hector. ἐπετοξάζοντο is the imperfect middle of ἐπιτοξάζομαι ‘shoot at with the bow’, and τιτυσκόμενοι ‘aiming’ is a participle that goes with ἰοῖσιν ‘with arrows’ (ἰός is ‘arrow’); λάεσσι is the epic dative plural of λᾶας ‘stone’, and ἔβαλλον the imperfect of βάλλω ‘strike, throw’. The imperfects show it going on until Agamemnon stops it.

sentences.t: αὐτὰρ ὃ μακρὸν ἄϋσεν ἄναξ ἀνδρῶν Ἀγαμέμνων·
sentences.tr: autar ho makron aÿsen anax andrōn Agamemnōn·
sentences.l: But he shouted loudly, lord of men Agamemnon:
sentences.i: But Agamemnon, lord of men, cried out loudly:
sentences.n: αὐτὰρ ὃ is ‘but he’ (ὃ the article as a pronoun), and ἄϋσεν is the aorist of ἀΰω ‘shout’, with the diaeresis marking the vowels as separate. μακρόν is an adverb, literally ‘long’, so ‘loudly’. ἄναξ ἀνδρῶν is the stock epithet ‘lord of men’.

sentences.t: ἴσχεσθ’ Ἀργεῖοι, μὴ βάλλετε κοῦροι Ἀχαιῶν·
sentences.tr: ischesth’ Argeioi, mē ballete kouroi Achaiōn·
sentences.l: “Hold back, Argives, do not strike, youths of the Achaeans;
sentences.i: “Hold back, Argives; do not strike, young men of the Achaeans;
sentences.n: ἴσχεσθ’ is ἴσχεσθε, the middle imperative of ἴσχω ‘hold back, stop’, and μὴ βάλλετε the present imperative with μή, ‘do not strike’. Ἀργεῖοι and κοῦροι Ἀχαιῶν (‘young men of the Achaeans’) are two forms of address for the same army.

sentences.t: στεῦται γάρ τι ἔπος ἐρέειν κορυθαίολος Ἕκτωρ.
sentences.tr: steutai gar ti epos ereein korythaiolos Hektōr.
sentences.l: for Hector of the glancing helmet claims some word to say.”
sentences.i: for Hector of the glancing helmet claims that he will say something.”
sentences.n: στεῦται is the present of στεῦμαι ‘claim, declare’, and it takes the future infinitive ἐρέειν (Attic ἐρεῖν) ‘to say’ with τι ἔπος ‘some word’. κορυθαίολος ‘of the glancing helmet’ is the stock epithet of Hector. The speech, and the part, end on this reason for stopping.
